newsitem.title: LEBANON: Syria underlines deepening Arab-Israeli divide.
newsitem.headline: Syria underlines deepening Arab-Israeli divide.

text.p: Syria underlined the wider crisis in the Middle East peace process on Friday, accusing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of "extremism and fanaticism" that has blocked any revival of negotiations.

The speech by President Hafez al-Assad, printed in Damascus to mark Army Day, came as Israel arrested Palestinians after Wednesday's suicide bombings of a Jerusalem market that killed 15 people, including the two attackers.

It also coincided with a visit by Assad to Tehran -- only his second trip to Iran since the Islamic revolution there in 1979 and apparently part of Assad's efforts to shore up support in the increasingly polarised region.

"We will not relinquish even a single tree in the Golan," Assad said when he arrived on Thursday in the Iranian capital, repeating his key demand for return of the Syrian land occupied by Israel since 1967.

Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani added that they had to discuss the increasing military links between Israel and Turkey -- seen by Damascus as a threatening step to encircle it -- and the Middle East economic summit scheduled for Qatar in November that is supposed to increase Israeli integration in the region.

"The circumstances of the region need a Syrian move," Rafsanjani said in coverage carried on Syrian state television. "We consider this initiative important to carry out an Arab-Iranian action that faces head on the anti-Arab and anti-Moslem alliance headed by Israel and the United States."

The Tehran talks, which came two days after Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met in Damascus with Assad, were a reminder that the search for Middle East peace since the election of Netanyahu in May 1996 has deteriorated on all fronts.
Syria's talks with the previous Israeli government had made little progress since peace negotiations began in 1991 -- and were suspended by Israel shortly before Netanyahu's Likud party victory.

But the new Israeli leader's rejection of the principle of trading occupied Arab land for peace, including Syria's Golan Heights, appeared to close off prospects of fresh negotiations. Israel's proposal for talks without conditions -- meaning no commitment to discuss return of the Golan -- has been rejected.

At the same time, Syria has become increasingly alarmed by growing links between Turkish and Israeli forces, backed by the United States. Plans for joint naval exercises this summer drew a condemnation from an Arab summit in Syria in June.

Assad, once isolated, has found increasing sympathy with other Arab leaders since Netanyahu's election. Last month Saudi Arabia endorsed his call for boycotting the Qatar summit, leaving Egypt as the most important Arab state still undecided.

In June Assad opened the Syria-Iraqi border for the first time since the start of the Iran-Iraq war in 1980, easing the U.S.-led isolation of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. Bus travel between the capitals began this week.

Divisions between potential allies of Syria remain deep. Syria joined the coalition, which included Saudi Arabia, that drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991. Iraq says Iran is still holding more than 20,000 Iraqi prisoners from their 1980-88 war.
But Netanyahu's drive to increase Jewish settlement of occupied Arab land -- especially in East Jerusalem -- triggered anger throughout the region as well as halting Israeli-Palestinian talks.
Even Arab states with close U.S. ties, such as Egypt and Jordan, have expressed fears that Israeli policies, unopposed by Washington, are pushing the Middle East toward more violence.

"We called for peace...and Israel under its current government responded by going far in extremism and fanaticism, reneging on all that had been achieved during the five years after the start of the process and undermining all efforts to revive it," Assad said for Army Day.

The Syrian leader said earlier this week he could see no hope of peace and in what has become a recurring pattern over the past year, Syrian and Israeli officials ended the week in an exchange of words over the possibility of war.
"If Netanyahu and his group are working to create war conditions, then Syria...knows how to defend itself," Major-General Hikmat Shihabi, Syrian army chief of staff, said on Thursday.
On Friday, Israel's ambassador to Washington, Eliahu Ben-Elissar replied: "They will not achieve anything by force. They can only lose everything."
